pumac-2009-algebra-b-02.title: Find the minimal polynomial
pumac-2009-algebra-b-02.body:
Let $x=\sqrt{3+\sqrt{3+\sqrt{3+\cdots}}}$. The expression under the first root is $3+x$ again, so $x^2=3+x$, i.e. $x^2-x-3=0$.

The roots of $t^2-t-3$ are $\frac{1\pm\sqrt{13}}2$, which are irrational, so $x$ is not a root of any monic linear polynomial with rational coefficients. Hence the least degree is $2$. A monic quadratic with rational coefficients having $x$ as a root is unique (the difference of two such would be a nonzero rational polynomial of degree at most $1$ vanishing at $x$), so $p(t)=t^2-t-3$.

$p(5)=25-5-3=17$.

**Answer: 17**

pumac-2009-algebra-b-03.title: Subtract two of the polynomials
pumac-2009-algebra-b-03.body:
A common root is a root of the difference of the first two polynomials: $(x^3+41x^2-49x-2009)-(x^3+5x^2-49x-245)=36x^2-1764=36(x^2-49)$. So the common root is $7$ or $-7$.

Test in the third polynomial: at $x=7$: $343+39\cdot 49-117\cdot 7-1435=343+1911-819-1435=0$. At $x=-7$: $-343+1911+819-1435=952\neq0$.

Also $x=7$ is a root of the first two: $343+2009-343-2009=0$ and $343+245-343-245=0$.

**Answer: 7**

pumac-2009-algebra-b-03.title: Rational root test
pumac-2009-algebra-b-03.body:
An integer root divides each constant term $2009=7^2\cdot41$, $245=5\cdot7^2$, $1435=5\cdot7\cdot41$. Their gcd is $7$, so the common root is among $\pm1,\pm7$. Checking, only $7$ works in all three.

**Answer: 7**

pumac-2009-algebra-b-04.title: Powers of $\sqrt2+\sqrt3$
pumac-2009-algebra-b-04.body:
Let $x=\sqrt2+\sqrt3$. Then $x^2=5+2\sqrt6$ and $x^3=x\cdot x^2=11\sqrt2+9\sqrt3$.

Try $ax^3+bx=\sqrt2$: the coefficient of $\sqrt2$ gives $11a+b=1$ and of $\sqrt3$ gives $9a+b=0$. So $a=\frac12$, $b=-\frac92$ and $$P(x)=\frac{x^3-9x}{2}.$$

Degree at least $3$: a rational polynomial $ax^2+bx+c$ of degree $\le2$ would give $a(5+2\sqrt6)+b(\sqrt2+\sqrt3)+c=\sqrt2$, and since $1,\sqrt2,\sqrt3,\sqrt6$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$ the coefficient of $\sqrt3$ forces $b=0$, then $\sqrt2$ cannot appear. So degree $3$ is least (and the cubic is unique).

$P(10)=\frac{1000-90}{2}=455$.

**Answer: 455**

pumac-2009-algebra-b-05.title: Substitute and bound
pumac-2009-algebra-b-05.body:
Put $a_i=x_i/i\ge0$. Then $\sum a_i\le 9$ and we maximise $\sum \frac{x_i^2}{i}=\sum i\,a_i^2$.

$$\sum i\,a_i^2\le 10\sum a_i^2\le 10\Big(\sum a_i\Big)^2\le 10\cdot 81=810.$$ (The middle step holds because all $a_i\ge0$, so the cross terms are non-negative.)

Equality holds for $a_{10}=9$ and all other $a_i=0$, i.e. $x_{10}=90$, giving $\frac{90^2}{10}=810$.

**Answer: 810**

pumac-2009-algebra-b-06.title: Show $120^\circ$ works and is smallest
pumac-2009-algebra-b-06.body:
**$120^\circ$ works:** $2^n\cdot120^\circ$ is congruent to $120^\circ$ or $240^\circ$ modulo $360^\circ$ (it alternates), and the cosine of both is $-\frac12<0$.

**Nothing smaller works.** Work modulo $360^\circ$. We need $\cos\alpha<0$, so $90^\circ<\alpha<270^\circ$. If $180^\circ<\alpha<270^\circ$ is good then $\alpha/2\in(90^\circ,135^\circ)$ is also good and smaller, and $\alpha=180^\circ$ fails ($\cos 2\alpha=1$). So a smallest good $\alpha$ lies in $(90^\circ,180^\circ)$.

Put $x=\alpha/90^\circ\in(1,2)$. Then $\cos2^n\alpha<0$ means $2^nx \bmod 4\in(1,3)$, so $\lfloor 2^nx\rfloor \bmod 4\in\{1,2\}$.

Write $x$ in base 4: $x=1.d_1d_2d_3\ldots$. For $n=2m$ the number $\lfloor4^mx\rfloor$ has last base-4 digit $d_m$, so every $d_m\in\{1,2\}$.

Suppose some digit is $2$, and let $d_m$ be the first one, so $d_1=\dots=d_{m-1}=1$. Then $N=\lfloor4^{m-1}x\rfloor\equiv1\pmod4$ and the fractional part of $4^{m-1}x$ is at least $0.2_4=\frac12$. Thus $\lfloor2\cdot4^{m-1}x\rfloor=2N+1\equiv3\pmod4$, contradicting the condition for $n=2m-1$.

Hence all digits equal $1$ and $x=1.111\ldots_4=\frac43$, i.e. $\alpha=120^\circ$ is the only good angle in $(90^\circ,180^\circ)$, so the smallest good angle is $120^\circ$.

**Answer: 120**

pumac-2009-algebra-b-07.title: Parity, then convexity
pumac-2009-algebra-b-07.body:
At $x=\pi$: $\sin^n x+\cos^n x=(-1)^n\ge \frac1n>0$ forces $n$ even, say $n=2m$.

Let $u=\sin^2x$, $v=\cos^2x$, so $u+v=1$. By convexity of $t\mapsto t^m$ (power mean), $$u^m+v^m\ge 2\Big(\frac{u+v}{2}\Big)^m=2^{1-m},$$ with equality at $\sin^2x=\cos^2x=\frac12$. So the minimum of $\sin^nx+\cos^nx$ is exactly $2^{1-m}$ and we need $2^{1-m}\ge\frac1{2m}$, i.e. $2^m\le4m$.

For $m=4$: $16\le16$ holds. For $m=5$: $32\le20$ fails, and $2^m>4m$ for all $m\ge5$. So the largest even $n$ is $2\cdot4=8$.

**Answer: 8**

pumac-2009-algebra-b-08.title: Determine $f(0)$, $f(1)$, $f(-1)$
pumac-2009-algebra-b-08.body:
$(h,k)=(0,0)$: $2f(0)=f(0)^2+1$, so $(f(0)-1)^2=0$ and $f(0)=1$.

$(h,k)=(1,-1)$: $f(0)+f(-1)=f(1)f(-1)+1$, so $f(-1)\,(f(1)-1)=0$.

**Case $f(1)=1$.** With $h=1$: $f(1+k)+f(k)=f(k)+1$, so $f(k+1)=1$ for all $k$: $f\equiv1$.

**Case $f(-1)=0$.** $(h,k)=(-1,-1)$ gives $f(-2)+f(1)=1$, and $(1,-2)$ gives $f(-1)+f(-2)=f(1)f(-2)+1$, i.e. $f(-2)=f(1)f(-2)+1$. Substituting $f(-2)=1-f(1)$: $(1-f(1))^2=1$, so $f(1)\in\{0,2\}$. With $h=1$ the equation reads $f(k+1)+f(k)=f(1)f(k)+1$.
- $f(1)=0$: $f(k+1)=1-f(k)$, and with $f(0)=1$ this gives $f(k)=1$ for even $k$ and $0$ for odd $k$.
- $f(1)=2$: $f(k+1)=f(k)+1$, so $f(k)=k+1$.

**Check.** $f\equiv1$: $1+1=1+1$. $f(k)=k+1$: $(h+k+1)+(hk+1)=(h+1)(k+1)+1$. Parity function: for $h,k$ both even both sides are $1+1=1\cdot1+1$; for one even and one odd, $h+k$ is odd and $hk$ even, so $0+1=0\cdot1+1$; for both odd, $h+k$ is even and $hk$ odd, so $1+0=0\cdot0+1$. All three work.

**Answer: 3**
